Laboratory incubation experiments with Bibron (Pseudophryne bibronii) conducted at a constant temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] have provided detailed insights into early developmental energetics. The initial energy reserve contained within each freshly laid, yolk-laden egg is approximately 65.03 J , a value that reflects the substantial maternal investment characteristic of this myobatrachid frog. At the moment of chorion rupture, the total energy remaining in the hatchling is partitioned into two distinct components: a somatic fraction of 31.69 J and a residual yolk fraction of 21.11 J, summing to 52.80 J . This energetic depletion over the incubation period is mirrored by a corresponding loss in dry mass, as the initial dry weight of the egg is 0.00268 g , whereas the hatchling emerges with a composite dry weight comprising a structural component of 0.00148 g and an unabsorbed yolk component of 0.00092 g, for a total of 0.00240 g . The difference between egg and hatchling dry mass underscores the metabolic costs incurred during embryonic development.

Following eclosion, the endotrophic tadpoles of Pseudophryne bibronii undergo a prolonged period of larval development before reaching metamorphic climax at a constant temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. Eclosion from the jelly-coated egg occurs after an incubation period of approximately 39 days [ab = approximately 39 days], after which the newly emerged larva measures just 0.58 cm [Lb = 0.58 cm] in total length at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. These free-swimming tadpoles remain dependent on their endogenous yolk reserves for a short period before the onset of exogenous feeding. The subsequent larval phase, encompassing the entirety of the filter-feeding and actively growing tadpole stages, culminates in metamorphosis after an average duration of 185 days  when maintained at this same thermal regime at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. By the time of metamorphic climax, the total length of the individual has increased dramatically, and the dry weight at metamorphosis is composed of a somatic mass of 0.02319 g combined with a tail-resorption component of 0.00117 g, yielding a total of 0.02436 g .

The post-metamorphic growth trajectory of Pseudophryne bibronii is characterized by a steady increase in body size that continues well into adulthood. The ultimate dry weight attained by fully grown adults in the field has been recorded at 0.2 g , a modest mass that is consistent with the species' small body size among Australian ground frogs. Correspondingly, the ultimate total length from snout to vent reaches approximately 3.2 cm [Li = approximately 3.2 cm], representing the asymptotic size that individuals approach after several years of growth. It is worth noting that the total length at puberty, the size at which individuals first become reproductively viable, is considerably smaller at 2.2 cm [Lp = 2.2 cm], indicating that sexual maturation occurs well before somatic growth ceases. This pattern of early maturation relative to final size is common among amphibians inhabiting unpredictable environments where the probability of surviving to a later, larger body size is uncertain.

Reproductive maturation and the timing of first breeding in Bibron have been examined under controlled laboratory conditions. At a stable temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], individuals reach first reproduction approximately 427 days after hatching [tR = approximately 427 days after hatching], when gravid females first deposit eggs following amplexus. The dry weight at puberty, measured in individuals that have just completed gonadal maturation, is approximately 0.15 g , which is substantially less than the ultimate dry weight of 0.2 g recorded in older adults. This disparity suggests that females may defer maximal reproductive allocation until they have accumulated additional somatic reserves. Once sexually mature, the maximum reproductive rate of captive females at this same temperature has been documented as 0.55 clutches per day [F_R_i = 0.55 clutches per day], a high frequency that likely reflects optimal provisioning in the absence of environmental constraints.

Long-term demographic studies of Pseudophryne bibronii in its native range have revealed a maximum lifespan that is remarkably extended for a small anuran. Under field conditions, the oldest documented individuals have been recorded living for up to 1,825 days [am = up to 1,825 days], which corresponds to approximately five years, when ambient thermal regimes approximate an average of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This considerable longevity, relative to many similarly sized amphibians, may be linked to the species' slow life-history pace, including the protracted larval development of 185 days  and the deferred age at first reproduction of approximately 427 days after hatching [tR = approximately 427 days after hatching] at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. Furthermore, the relatively high energy content at metamorphosis, measured at 464.02 J , provides juveniles with a substantial energetic buffer that may enhance survivorship during the critical period of terrestrial transition. These life-history traits collectively suggest a bet-hedging strategy adapted to the stochastic environmental conditions of southern Australian habitats.
